misconceptions.statement: Iron in the body is the same metal as iron nails and tools.
misconceptions.why: The same word 'iron' is used for the metal and the nutrient.
misconceptions.fix: The body needs iron only as a tiny amount of a mineral in food; eating iron metal or rust is harmful and not a source.

probe.question: Will sucking on an iron nail or cooking rusty iron pieces help cure anaemia?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: The more iron we eat, the healthier we become, so large amounts are always good.
misconceptions.why: Students think a nutrient that is good must be good in any quantity.
misconceptions.fix: The body needs only a small, fixed amount of iron; too much iron from tablets can be poisonous.

probe.question: A girl takes many iron tablets daily without advice. Is this safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, more iron is always better

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Haemoglobin carries food to the body cells.
misconceptions.why: Blood is known as the transport fluid, so students assume it carries everything the same way.
misconceptions.fix: Haemoglobin in red blood cells carries oxygen; digested food is carried mainly in the plasma.

probe.question: What does haemoglobin carry?
probe.wrong_answer: Digested food and energy to the cells

misconceptions.root_belief: one carrier does every transport job
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student ideas about blood and circulation

misconceptions.statement: Haemoglobin makes the body produce energy by itself.
misconceptions.why: Students link oxygen and energy and skip the role of food and cells.
misconceptions.fix: Haemoglobin only carries oxygen; cells use oxygen to release energy from food.

probe.question: Where does the energy come from when haemoglobin delivers oxygen?

misconceptions.root_belief: one thing alone produces the whole effect

misconceptions.statement: Blood is red because it has lots of red food colour or iron rust in it.
misconceptions.why: Students link redness with rust and everyday colouring.
misconceptions.fix: Blood is red because of haemoglobin, a protein containing iron, inside red blood cells.

probe.question: Why is blood red?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it contains rust-like iron particles

misconceptions.root_belief: colour comes from a visible coloured substance

misconceptions.statement: Anaemia means a person has too little blood.
misconceptions.why: 'Lack of blood' is the common way anaemia is described in daily speech.
misconceptions.fix: Anaemia means the blood has too little haemoglobin or too few healthy red cells, not too little blood volume.

probe.question: What is anaemia?
probe.wrong_answer: Having less quantity of blood in the body

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: teacher-reported and diagnostic-test studies on blood and health concepts

misconceptions.statement: Anaemia means the blood has no white blood cells.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up red and white cells.
misconceptions.fix: Anaemia is about haemoglobin and red blood cells; white cells fight germs.

probe.question: Which blood part is low in anaemia?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar-sounding parts have the same job

misconceptions.statement: Anaemia spreads from one person to another like a cold.
misconceptions.why: Students treat every illness as caused by germs.
misconceptions.fix: Anaemia is a deficiency problem, not an infection, so it cannot spread by touch, air or sharing food.

probe.question: Can sitting next to an anaemic friend give you anaemia?

misconceptions.root_belief: all diseases are caused by germs
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's ideas about disease causation (germ theory overgeneralised)

misconceptions.statement: Anaemia can be recognised only when a person is very sick and in bed.
misconceptions.why: Students expect diseases to look dramatic.
misconceptions.fix: Mild anaemia can show as slight tiredness, pale skin or nails; a blood test for haemoglobin confirms it.

probe.question: A girl is often tired and pale but goes to school. Can she be anaemic?
probe.wrong_answer: No, she would be in bed if anaemic

misconceptions.root_belief: a real problem is always obvious

misconceptions.statement: Anyone who looks pale or is tired must have anaemia.
misconceptions.why: Students treat a symptom as proof of one cause.
misconceptions.fix: Tiredness and paleness can have many causes; anaemia is confirmed by a haemoglobin blood test.

probe.question: A boy is tired after a late night and looks pale. Is it surely anaemia?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, these are signs of anaemia

misconceptions.root_belief: one sign means one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Feeling breathless during a run means the lungs are damaged, never a blood problem.
misconceptions.why: Breathing is linked only to lungs.
misconceptions.fix: If blood has less haemoglobin, it carries less oxygen, so the person feels breathless and tires quickly even with healthy lungs.

probe.question: A girl with healthy lungs gets breathless climbing stairs. Which part may be the problem?

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Anaemia in girls is caused by menstruation being a disease.
misconceptions.why: Menstruation is misunderstood as illness.
misconceptions.fix: Menstruation is normal; blood loss only raises the body's need for iron, so girls need iron-rich food.

probe.question: Why are adolescent girls more at risk of anaemia?

misconceptions.root_belief: natural changes are illnesses

misconceptions.statement: Only girls can get anaemia; boys never need extra iron.
misconceptions.why: Anaemia messages are aimed mostly at girls and women.
misconceptions.fix: Boys also grow fast in adolescence and can be anaemic, though girls are at higher risk.

probe.question: Can a 14-year-old boy have anaemia?

misconceptions.root_belief: a risk group is the only group affected

misconceptions.statement: Anaemia is caused only by not eating enough iron.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks stress diet, so students think nothing else matters.
misconceptions.fix: Hookworm infection, blood loss, malaria and poor absorption can also cause anaemia.

probe.question: A child eats well but has hookworms. Can she be anaemic?
probe.wrong_answer: No, she gets enough iron from food

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Only meat and eggs have iron, so vegetarians cannot get enough.
misconceptions.why: Animal foods are widely advertised as 'strong' foods.
misconceptions.fix: Green leafy vegetables, jaggery, pulses, ragi and other millets give iron; eating them with vitamin C foods helps.

probe.question: Name an iron-rich food a vegetarian can eat.

misconceptions.root_belief: only animal foods give strength

misconceptions.statement: Spinach contains so much iron that eating it once instantly cures anaemia.
misconceptions.why: Popeye-type media stories exaggerate spinach.
misconceptions.fix: Iron-rich foods must be eaten regularly over weeks to months to restore haemoglobin; one meal cannot cure anaemia.

probe.question: How soon will one plate of spinach cure anaemia?

misconceptions.root_belief: one big dose gives instant result

misconceptions.statement: Milk is the best food for preventing anaemia because it is a complete food.
misconceptions.why: Milk is called a complete or perfect food.
misconceptions.fix: Milk has very little iron; relying only on milk can cause anaemia in children, so iron-rich foods are needed too.

probe.question: A girl drinks lots of milk but eats few greens or pulses. Is she safe from anaemia?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, milk gives all nutrients including iron

misconceptions.root_belief: a complete food contains everything in plenty
misconceptions.source_hint: public health nutrition guidance on iron deficiency in children with milk-heavy diets

misconceptions.statement: Vitamin C itself contains the iron that builds haemoglobin.
misconceptions.why: Students merge the two nutrients mentioned together.
misconceptions.fix: Vitamin C does not contain iron; it helps the body absorb more iron from plant foods eaten with it.

probe.question: Why add lemon juice to a spinach meal?

misconceptions.root_belief: things named together do the same job

misconceptions.statement: If iron is in the food, all of it automatically enters the blood.
misconceptions.why: Students assume eating equals absorbing.
misconceptions.fix: Only part of the iron in food is absorbed, and how much depends on the food combination, such as vitamin C present or tea.

probe.question: Two meals have the same iron. Will the body get the same iron from both?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all iron is absorbed equally

misconceptions.root_belief: what goes in is fully used

misconceptions.statement: Drinking tea or coffee with meals gives extra iron and strength.
misconceptions.why: Tea is considered an energising everyday drink.
misconceptions.fix: Tannins and similar substances in tea and coffee reduce iron absorption, so it is better to drink them between meals, not with meals.

probe.question: Is tea with lunch good for anaemia?

misconceptions.root_belief: a common habit must be healthy

misconceptions.statement: Tea blocks iron only if it is very strong or has no milk.
misconceptions.why: Students think only the dark colour matters.
misconceptions.fix: Tea reduces iron absorption in any strength, so keep a gap of an hour or two from meals.

probe.question: Is weak tea with a meal harmless for iron absorption?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, only strong tea blocks iron

misconceptions.root_belief: only a large amount has any effect

misconceptions.statement: Iron-folic acid tablets are medicine only for sick people and are unsafe for healthy girls.
misconceptions.why: Tablets are mostly linked to treating illness.
misconceptions.fix: Government programmes give weekly iron-folic acid tablets to adolescents to prevent anaemia, and they are safe when taken as advised.

probe.question: Should a healthy schoolgirl take the weekly IFA tablet given at school?
probe.wrong_answer: No, tablets are only for sick people

misconceptions.root_belief: medicine is only for the sick

misconceptions.statement: Taking iron tablets means we no longer need to eat iron-rich foods.
misconceptions.why: Tablets seem a complete replacement for food.
misconceptions.fix: Tablets support but do not replace a balanced diet that includes iron-rich foods.

probe.question: After taking IFA tablets, can a girl skip greens and pulses?

misconceptions.root_belief: a supplement can replace a whole diet
